No, the penalty likely doesn't apply. Under the Rule of 55, distributions from the 401(k) of the employer you separated from are exempt from the 10% early-withdrawal penalty if you left in or after the calendar year you turned 55. At 56, you almost certainly qualify.

**Fastest route:** request a cash distribution directly from that plan's administrator, usually through the provider's website or by phone. Processing typically takes days to a couple of weeks, depending on the plan.

**Caveats:**
- **Don't roll it to an IRA first.** The exception applies only to money still in the plan of the employer you left. Once it's in an IRA, the penalty returns until 59½.
- **It covers only that employer's plan.** 401(k)s from earlier jobs don't qualify unless they were rolled into this plan before you separated.
- **Income tax still applies.** The plan must withhold 20% for federal tax on a cash distribution. That's a prepayment, not the final bill, so you settle up at filing. State tax may also apply.
- **Plan rules vary.** Some plans only allow a lump sum, and some restrict partial withdrawals. Check the summary plan description or ask the administrator.
- **Consider the tax bracket.** A full lump sum in one year can push you into a much higher bracket. If you don't need all of it at once, spreading withdrawals across tax years may cut the tax noticeably. That's the main reason not to take it all at once.

If any of your money is in a prior employer's plan or an IRA, tell me and I'll cover the alternative, a 72(t) SEPP plan, which has stricter rules.
